---
title: "What a group is, and what it is for"
description: "The definition, the first examples that matter for physics, and Lagrange's theorem as a first taste of structure."
date: 2026-11-19
categories: [groups, foundations]
---

A group is the mathematical object that captures *symmetry* — not any particular
symmetry, but the way symmetries compose. Every example in this note comes from
asking "what transformations leave this thing alone?" and then noticing that the
answers can be combined and undone.

## The definition

::: {#def-group}
## Group

A **group** is a set $G$ together with a binary operation
$G \times G \to G$, written $(g, h) \mapsto gh$, such that

1. **Associativity.** $(gh)k = g(hk)$ for all $g, h, k \in G$.
2. **Identity.** There is an element $e \in G$ with $eg = ge = g$ for all $g$.
3. **Inverses.** For each $g \in G$ there is a $g^{-1} \in G$ with
   $g g^{-1} = g^{-1} g = e$.

If in addition $gh = hg$ for all $g, h$, the group is **abelian**.
:::

Nothing in @def-group says the elements are functions, but in practice they
almost always are: $G$ acts on some space $X$ and the product is composition.
Associativity is then automatic, which is why it never feels like a real axiom.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why no closure axiom?

Many textbooks list "closure" ($gh \in G$) as a fourth axiom. Here it is built
into the phrase *binary operation $G \times G \to G$*. It is the same
requirement; it just lives in the type of the map rather than in a separate
bullet.
:::

## Examples worth keeping

The examples below are the ones that keep returning in physics.

- $\Z$ under addition, and $\Z/n\Z$ under addition mod $n$: the simplest
  infinite and finite abelian groups.
- $S_n$, the permutations of $\set{1, \dots, n}$ under composition. Non-abelian
  for $n \ge 3$. Identical-particle statistics live here.
- $\GL(n, \C)$, the invertible $n \times n$ complex matrices under matrix
  multiplication. Almost every group a physicist meets is a subgroup of this
  one.
- $\SO(3) = \set{R \in \GL(3,\R) : R^{\mathsf T} R = I,\ \det R = 1}$,
  rotations of three-dimensional space.
- $\SU(2) = \set{U \in \GL(2,\C) : U^\dagger U = I,\ \det U = 1}$, which
  will turn out to be a *double cover* of $\SO(3)$ — the reason spin-$\half$
  exists. That story is told in
  [SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3)](../lie-theory/su2-covers-so3.qmd).

::: {#exm-dihedral}
## The dihedral group

The symmetries of a regular $n$-gon form the dihedral group $D_n$, of order
$2n$: $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections. It is generated by a rotation $r$ of
angle $2\pi/n$ and a single reflection $s$, subject to
$r^n = s^2 = e$ and $s r s = r^{-1}$. The last relation says that reflecting,
rotating, and reflecting back rotates the other way — which is exactly what a
mirror does.
:::

## A first structural theorem

Groups are rigid objects, and the first sign of that rigidity is that the size
of a subgroup is severely constrained.

::: {#thm-lagrange}
## Lagrange

Let $G$ be a finite group and $H \le G$ a subgroup. Then $\abs{H}$ divides
$\abs{G}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $g \in G$, the **left coset** $gH = \set{gh : h \in H}$ has exactly
$\abs{H}$ elements, because $h \mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H \to gH$ (its
inverse is $x \mapsto g^{-1}x$). Two cosets $gH$ and $g'H$ are either equal or
disjoint: if $x \in gH \cap g'H$ then $x = gh_1 = g'h_2$, so
$g = g' h_2 h_1^{-1} \in g'H$ and hence $gH \subseteq g'H$, and symmetrically.
Every element $g$ lies in its own coset $gH$. So $G$ is a disjoint union of
cosets, each of size $\abs{H}$, and
$$
\abs{G} = [G : H] \cdot \abs{H},
$$ {#eq-lagrange}
where $[G:H]$ is the number of distinct cosets.
:::

The ratio $[G:H]$ in @eq-lagrange is the **index** of $H$ in $G$, and the set
of cosets $G/H$ is the first quotient construction we meet. When $H$ is
*normal* ($gHg^{-1} = H$ for all $g$) the cosets themselves form a group, and
that is the quotient group $G/H$ — which is how $\SO(3)$ will be built from
$\SU(2)$.

::: {#exr-lagrange}
Use @thm-lagrange to show that a group of prime order $p$ is cyclic, i.e.
generated by any one of its non-identity elements.
:::

## Where this is going

Three ideas from this note carry all the way to QFT. Groups act on things; the
things they act on are vector spaces (that is representation theory); and
quotienting by a normal subgroup is how one symmetry group is obtained from
another. The standard references for this material are Artin [@artin2011] for
the mathematics and Zee [@zee2016] for the physicist's point of view.
